One program.
Five routes.

School, theme, and practical information connect the series. A vertical spine, split field, arch, diagonal planes, or open sage ground gives each poster its own spatial character.

A compositional toolkit

Skills.md

Six practical moves for building a poster that feels ordered, expressive, and easy to read. Inspired by architectural thinking; written for this poster system.

Download skills.md ↓
01 / HIERARCHY

Set a readable order

Let the program, school, theme, and practical details occupy distinct levels. Keep the schedule easy to find.

02 / ALIGNMENT

Give alignment a job

Use a strong line or edge to organize the type. The stone poster uses a vertical spine; lavender uses a divider.

03 / SPACE

Balance open and occupied space

Let the sage field breathe; let the lavender split carry denser information. Balance through scale and placement.

04 / SHAPE

Let shape support the subject

Use a wave to soften, an arch to frame, or a diagonal to add motion. Choose one main gesture per composition.

05 / COLOR

Keep color roles simple

Begin with a ground and readable ink; reserve brighter marks for useful emphasis. Preserve the source palettes.

06 / TYPE

Check type at poster size

Let the display title lead, then step down for school, place, time, and reservation details.

07 / TRIM

Treat the edge as structure

Keep essential copy safely inside the trim; make rules, cut strokes, and corner marks deliberate.

REVIEW

Order → space → shape → type → print check

Keep the five posters connected by content while protecting each one's distinct layout.

Five routes through one Urban Studies program
The posters share Urban Studies, School of Spatial Design, and City / Memory / Material. They differ in where type sits, how empty space works, and which large shape organizes the page.

          
The variations
  • 01 — Datum & wave: warm stone, a tall vertical title, a long rule, and a soft lower transition.
  • 02 — Lavender split: offset text areas, a central divider, and small floating strokes on a lavender field.
  • 03 — Charcoal arch: a pale arc and outlined circles frame compact centered type against a dark ground.
  • 04 — Ivory diagonals: pale layered planes, colored diamonds, and cropped strokes create movement in open space.
  • 05 — Sage field: a muted ground and compact type grouping make the most restrained direction.

          
What connects them
The school name, program theme, and practical details repeat across the set. Heavy condensed lettering provides continuity while the wave, split, arch, diagonal, and open field establish different spatial orders.

          
Choosing a direction
The stone poster emphasizes its vertical spine; lavender makes the clearest split; charcoal creates the quietest focal stage; ivory feels the most mobile; and sage offers the most restraint. The right choice depends on where the poster will be seen and how much attention the program should draw.
